title: The Coach and the Fly
text:
On a steep, sandy road, in the full heat of the sun, six strong horses were struggling to drag a heavy coach uphill. The passengers, a woman, a monk and some old men, had all climbed out to lighten the load. The horses were sweating and exhausted.

A fly arrived. It buzzed around the horses and stung one, then another, as though urging them on. It landed on the shaft, then on the coachman's nose. Whenever the coach moved forward a little, the fly took the credit. It zipped back and forth like a sergeant on a battlefield, and it complained loudly that it alone was doing everything, while the others were no help at all. The monk was saying his prayers, and the woman was singing. What a time to sing!

At last, after a great struggle, the horses reached the top of the hill. The fly settled down, satisfied. Now, it said, let us take a breath. I have worked so hard to get you all up here. So, horses, pay me for my trouble.

La Fontaine adds that there are people like this everywhere, who bustle around other people's work, make themselves seem indispensable, and are only a nuisance.
lesson: Busy noise near a task is not the same as doing it. Notice who is actually pulling the load, and be wary of the one who complains loudest and claims the credit.
people: A fly, six horses, a coachman, passengers
source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book VII, The Coach and the Fly (Le Coche et la Mouche), 1678
